source_refs.note: Book p. 241-243: 8.3.4 Newton-Raphson Method, Figure 8.6, tangent derivation of the formula, steps, Example 5

blocks.text: The Newton–Raphson Method is a numerical method used to find an approximate real root of a nonlinear equation \(f(x) = 0\). This method works by drawing a tangent to the curve \(y = f(x)\) at a point near the root and using the point where this tangent crosses the \(x\)-axis as a better approximation of the root. The initial guess chosen is based on a sign-change interval.

Since this method requires the function to be differentiable (having a slope of tangent), it usually reaches a good approximation faster than the Bisection or Regula-Falsi methods. The derivative of \(f\) should not be zero near the root. This method does not rely directly on the Location of Root Theorem (LRT).

blocks.alt: Graph of an increasing curve y = f(x) bending downwards. The point (x0, f(x0)) is well below the x-axis; the tangent there cuts the axis at x1. The tangent at (x1, f(x1)) cuts the axis at x2, very close to the root c where the curve crosses the axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.6: Newton–Raphson, tangents at x0 and x1 meeting the x-axis at x1 and x2 near the root c (original drawing after the textbook's figure; plotted for f(x) = ln x - 1 from x0 = 1)

blocks.text: Suppose \(x_0\) is an initial guess for the root of \(f(x) = 0\), where:

The slope of the tangent line to the curve \(y = f(x)\) at the point \((x_0, f(x_0))\) is given by \(f'(x_0)\). Draw a tangent to the curve at this point (see Figure 8.6). The equation of the tangent line is:

blocks.text_alt: y minus f of x nought equals f dash of x nought times x minus x nought

blocks.text: This tangent intersects the \(x\)-axis at \(x = x_1\). Substituting \(y = 0\) and \(x = x_1\) gives:

blocks.text_alt: 0 minus f of x nought equals f dash of x nought times x 1 minus x nought
x 1 equals x nought minus f of x nought over f dash of x nought

blocks.text: Similarly, if we draw a tangent at \(x = x_1\), its \(x\)-intercept \(x_2\) is:

blocks.text_alt: x 2 equals x 1 minus f of x 1 over f dash of x 1

blocks.text: Repeating this process produces a sequence of \(x\)-intercepts:

blocks.text_alt: x n plus 1 equals x n minus f of x n over f dash of x n, n equals 0, 1, 2 and so on, with f dash of x n not zero

blocks.text: (\(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)). This is the Newton–Raphson formula, used to approximate the root of \(f(x) = 0\) iteratively.

From Figure 8.5, it is clear that each new approximation \(x_{n+1}\) is closer to the root, \(x = c\), than the previous one \(x_n\). If there exists some non-negative integer \(m\) such that \(x_{m+1} - x_m\) is closed to zero, then \(x_m\) will be the desired root, i.e. \(|f(x_m)| \approx 0\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: "From Figure 8.5" should be "From Figure 8.6" (Figure 8.5 is the Regula-Falsi figure), and "closed to zero" should be "close to zero".

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The step from \(0 - f(x_0) = f'(x_0)(x_1 - x_0)\) to \(x_1\): divide both sides by \(f'(x_0)\) (allowed because \(f'(x_0) \ne 0\)) to get \(x_1 - x_0 = -\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x_0)}\), then add \(x_0\).
Why \(f'(x) \ne 0\)? A zero slope means a horizontal tangent, which never meets the x-axis; the formula would divide by zero. A very small \(f'(x_n)\) gives a huge jump away from the root.
Why it is fast: near the root the curve is almost a straight line, and the tangent follows it closely, so the number of correct decimals roughly doubles at each step.

items:
Prepare the equation: Write the given equation in the form \(f(x) = 0\). Choose an initial approximation \(x_0\) from the interval where the function changes sign and ensure that:
(i) \(f(x)\) is differentiable within this interval.   (ii) \(f'(a) \ne 0\) near \(x_0\).

Set up the formula: \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\), \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\)
Use this to compute successive approximations.
Check for convergence: If \(|f(x_{n+1})| \approx 0\), then stop.
Conclude the root: \(x = x_{n+1}\) is the root correct to the desired accuracy.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Step 1(ii) prints \(f'(a) \ne 0\) near \(x_0\). There is no \(a\) in this method; it should be \(f'(x) \ne 0\) near \(x_0\).

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: Use Newton-Raphson method to find a root of \(f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 + 10x - 20\) correct to two decimal places.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 + 10x - 20\).
To find: a root correct to 2 decimal places.
Method: Newton–Raphson: tangent steps \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\) from a starting value inside an interval of sign change. Calculator fixed to 3 decimal places.

Choose initial approximation
\[f(1) = -7 < 0,\quad f(2) = 16 > 0\]
\[f(c) = \lim_{x \to c}(x^3 + 2x^2 + 10x - 20)\]
for every \(c \in [1, 2]\).
\(\Rightarrow\) is continuous on the interval of sign change \([1, 2]\).
\(\Rightarrow\) Root lies in the interval \([1, 2]\). Take the initial guess \(x_0 = 1.500\).
Why: the LRT puts a root in \([1, 2]\); its midpoint is a sensible starting value.

Derivative
\[f'(x) = 3x^2 + 4x + 10\]
\(f'\) exists and \(f'(x) \ne 0\) around \(x_0 = 1.5\) \(\Rightarrow\) Newton–Raphson method can be applied.
Why: in fact \(3x^2 + 4x + 10 > 0\) for every \(x\) (its discriminant \(16 - 120\) is negative), so the tangent is never horizontal.

Perform iterations: \(x_0 = 1.5\)
\[f(1.5) = 3.375 + 4.500 + 15 - 20\]
\[= 2.875 \ne 0\]
Why: \(x_0\) is not yet a root, so we iterate.

Iteration 2
\[f'(1.374) \approx 21.160\]
\[x_2 = 1.374 - \dfrac{0.110}{21.160} \approx 1.369\]
\[f(x_2) = f(1.369) \approx 0.002\]
Why: the next tangent step; \(x_2\) changes only in the third decimal place.

Stop iterations
\[|f(1.369)| \approx 0.002 < 0.01\]
Why: the book stops here (see the correction below).

Conclude the root
\[x \approx 1.37\]
accurate to two decimal places.

Check:
\[f(1.365) = -0.0802 < 0\]
\[f(1.375) = 0.1309 > 0\]
The root lies between 1.365 and 1.375, so it rounds to 1.37.

blocks.caption: Example 5 iterations in one table (our summary, 3 decimal places; f(1.369) corrected to 0.004)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
1. "\(\Rightarrow\) is continuous on the interval of sign change" leaves out \(f\): it should be "\(\Rightarrow f\) is continuous on \([1, 2]\)".
2. \(f(1.369) = 1.369^3 + 2(1.369)^2 + 10(1.369) - 20 = 2.5657 + 3.7483 + 13.69 - 20 = 0.0040\), not 0.002.
3. The stopping test should use the 2-decimal tolerance: \(|f(1.369)| \approx 0.004 < 0.005\), not \(< 0.01\). The conclusion \(x \approx 1.37\) is still correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Newton–Raphson formula: \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\), the x-intercept of the tangent at \((x_n, f(x_n))\).
2. Conditions: \(f\) differentiable near the root and \(f'(x) \ne 0\) there; start with \(x_0\) inside an interval of sign change.
3. Stop when \(|f(x_{n+1})|\) is below the tolerance (0.005 for 2 d.p.).
4. Usually the fastest of the three methods (Example 5: two iterations).
5. Unlike bisection and Regula-Falsi, the root is not trapped in an interval, so a poor \(x_0\) can lead away from the root.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(x_{n+1} = x_n + \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\): the sign is minus.
2. Differentiating wrongly, e.g. \(\frac{d}{dx}(2x^2) = 2x\) instead of \(4x\); check \(f'(x)\) before iterating.
3. Stopping because \(x_{n+1}\) and \(x_n\) agree to 2 decimals without checking \(|f(x_{n+1})|\) against the tolerance.
4. Using degree mode for trigonometric functions.
